title: Observe Technologies' camera AI registers behavioral change when gill disease hits two Scottish salmon farms
summary: University of Stirling study, 2023 season: fish activity rose from 25.6% to 43.6% (Farm A) and 24.9% to 32.6% (Farm B) after gill health deteriorated; proliferative gill disease drove it.
account: Researchers at the University of Stirling's Institute of Aquaculture, with co-authors from Observe Technologies (Richmond, UK) and Innovate UK funding in partnership with Observe and AKVA Group, applied Observe's algorithm, a patented convolutional neural network (EP3644717), to feed-camera video in every cage at two commercial Atlantic salmon marine farms in Scotland, with 5 and 4 extra cameras in one cage per farm. The algorithm outputs “activity” (%), combining fish abundance, speed and shoal cohesion; gill health, operational welfare indicators, mortality and specific feeding rate were scored weekly. Data were collected from 10 May to 10 September 2023 at Farm A and 22 June to 13 October 2023 at Farm B. Gill health issues arose at both farms in summer 2023: mean activity in the two months before was 25.6 ± 10.5% (A) and 24.9 ± 7.0% (B) and rose for two months afterwards to 43.6 ± 15.1% and 32.6 ± 9.6%, with fish moving to the center of the cage; a mixed model found proliferative gill disease the main driver. The paper proposes behavior as a non-invasive welfare indicator; it does not report an alert preceding diagnosis or a changed treatment. The date is the end of Farm B's data collection.
purpose: Extract group behavior (abundance, speed, shoal cohesion) from feed-camera video as a non-invasive indicator of fish health and welfare.
system: Observe Technologies behavioral monitoring algorithm (patented convolutional neural network, EP3644717)
deployer: Two commercial Atlantic salmon marine farms in Scotland, studied by the University of Stirling

ratings.reason: Gill disease was scored weekly by conventional means; the paper does not report any farm decision changed by the activity signal.
No outcome for farm staff or fish welfare beyond the behavioral correlation is documented.

ai_role.statement: The vendor's neural network quantified a behavioral response that coincided with gill disease already identified by weekly scoring; the study shows correlation, not an alert that changed what happened. Vendor staff co-authored the peer-reviewed paper.

evidence.citation: Burke M, Nikolic D, Fabry P, Rishi H, Telfer T, Rey Planellas S. Precision farming in aquaculture: assessing gill health in Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar) using a non-invasive, AI-driven behavioural monitoring approach in commercial farms. Aquaculture Science and Management 2:15 (2025). doi:10.1186/s44365-025-00020-8
evidence.title: Precision farming in aquaculture: assessing gill health in Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar) using a non-invasive, AI-driven behavioural monitoring approach in commercial farms
evidence.quote: After gill health was compromised, the activity rose significantly for two months in all cages with a mean of 43.6 ± 15.1% and 32.6 ± 9.6%, respectively.

produced_by: Feed cameras in all cages plus 4–5 extra cameras in one cage per farm
Weekly gill scoring, welfare indicators, mortality and feeding-rate records
A summer 2023 gill-health episode at both farms
must_hold: Gill disease severe enough to alter shoaling and distribution
Camera coverage of the cage volume

headline: Observe's AI registers salmon activity rising with gill disease
metric: fish activity rose from 25.6% to 43.6% (Farm A) and 24.9% to 32.6% (Farm B)

later.note: No later report on the Observe algorithm's use on these or other farms after the 2023 season was found.

revisions.change: Record drafted from the cited sources.

claim_basis: One independent peer-reviewed study is on file. There is no finding by a regulator or court.
